s04p.slug: SUNDAY · 11:20 AM · ST. CHARLES AVENUE — CARROLLTON
s04p.music: Professor Longhair — “Go to the Mardi Gras”
body: The piano gets to them before the parade does. It comes out of two speakers somebody has propped on the sills of an upstairs window across the avenue, a left hand rolling downhill and a right hand tripping over it on purpose, and a man’s voice laid on top that would rather you heard it than understood it. They left Remy’s Suburban in a stranger’s driveway six blocks back, on Remy’s word that he knew the man, and now they come out of a side street onto the neutral ground, the long green strip down the middle of St. Charles Avenue, where the streetcar tracks run empty and are being stood on, and the ladders stand along the curb in rows with a kid’s seat bolted to the top of each and a kid strapped into it. A family under a pop-up tent has held the same twenty feet since six o’clock with a gas grill, an ice chest and a sign taped to the tent pole, MAMA’S SPOT.

The sky is thin and bright and just cold enough for coats, and everything under it is black and gold: jerseys, wigs, a baby in a bib, a man’s beard dyed to match. The parade is an hour early on account of the game, and the avenue is talking about the game anyway. The air smells of charcoal and spilled Abita and, underneath, the river. Manning’s name goes by on the wind about every fourth sentence, said like the name of a weather system. The last parade Jack stood at was Memorial Day on Market Street, the VFW and the Mooney band and two fire trucks, with applause as polite as a church’s. Nothing was thrown at anyone. Here a man on a porch rail across the way is already crying, with a beer in his hand, at nothing yet.

Remy plants the milk crate by a hydrant, and the first float comes down on them at the speed of a man walking a dog: a flatbed under crepe paper and plywood, three tiers high, with masked riders on every tier in satin and foil and, over the satin, Saints jerseys. The one on top is swaying with a plastic cup. He points a gold glove at nobody in particular and flings a double handful of beads at the crowd. “He’s gonna be on Bourbon by five,” Remy says, “and he don’t even know it yet.”

Laney is up on the crate before the beads land. She’s in a Saints jersey of Tess’s that comes to her knees, belted into a dress, with her sunglasses pushed up into her hair and both arms in the air. “Throw me something, *mister*!” It goes up the avenue in a Dallas soprano built to carry over a brass band and survive a key change, and the rider on the second tier turns his entire mask her way. The beads come down in a long rope and she takes them out of the air with one hand, and a pink cup with the other, and a stuffed football off her shoulder, and hops down and puts the armful into the lap of a girl on the nearest ladder. “Here, sugar. You’re going to want to hang on to those.” She is back on the crate with her arms up before the girl has finished saying thank you. “In Dallas,” she tells the avenue, “a parade is a Shriner on a tiny motorcycle and a judge waving. No one throws anything at you. I have been lied to my entire life.”
“Purple’s justice,” Remy tells Margot, who has asked. “Green’s faith. Gold’s power.”
“Rex assigned the meanings in the 1890s,” Margot says. “Before that they were colors.”
“Where do y’all keep her?” Remy asks Jack.
Josie has taken Margot in hand. “You can’t just stand there. They don’t throw to people standing there.”
“I’m attending as an observer.”
“Observers don’t get beads.”
“Observers get the footnote.”

“It’s not a gift if you don’t holler, it’s a delivery,” says Josie, and Margot folds her arms inside the long black coat and declines, on principle, and watches a marching band come around the bend in maroon wool and white plumes, sousaphones bobbing, the drum line stepping on every second beat. Beside Jack, Jude has stood at his left elbow since the Suburban with his hands in his jacket pockets and said nothing, and he watches the band too. By the third float Jack has understood it as company.

On the next ladder over, a nine-year-old in a Brees jersey that comes to his shins is working the crowd from his seat on top. His mother stands under him with one hand on a rung. “Dominic, save your voice, baby, we got a *game*.” Dominic does not save his voice. He fills from the bottom up and lets go a THROW ME SOMETHING, MISTER you could land a plane by, and the rider on the nearest float swings around and fires a cup and a strand of beads that wraps his head twice.
Laney, down off her crate, pushes her sunglasses onto her nose to look at him. “That child has projection.”
“He’s from Gentilly,” says Josie. “They start ’em early.”
“Tell him he’s in my throwing lane,” Laney says to Theo, with her eyes on the next float, and it takes Jack a second to find out she means him.
“He’s standing right here,” says Theo.
“I know exactly where he is.”

Jack takes a step to the left. Theo has been filming since the stranger’s driveway, in the camel coat, the iPhone held out at arm’s length like a menu he can’t read, and on the fourth float Jack glances over at the screen and the screen is looking at him.
“That’s me.”
“Hm?” Theo doesn’t lower it.
“Your phone. That’s me.”
“Context,” says Theo.
“Context for what?”
“The floats.”
“The floats are behind me.”
“That’s what makes it context.” He keeps filming. A float goes by, and a dance troupe in gold sequins, and Theo says, easy, to the screen: “How was Mass?”
“I went up.”
“I know. I was in the pew.”
The drum line goes by with nothing on it. Then Theo swings the phone off Jack and onto the band, and holds it there, and studies the sousaphones with a concentration that would get him a scholarship.
“You’re filming a tuba.”
“Sousaphone. Different range.”

Behind them a rider on the next float is throwing medallion beads, plastic ones the size of a jar lid, and Josie, who has said all she has to, drops her arms and stops coaching. Margot takes her hands out of her coat. “Throw me something, mister,” she says. It is perfect. It is a low, carrying contralto with every consonant in place, and the rider turns round from three other people and hits her in the face with a medallion. Her glasses go crooked. The strand settles round her neck on its own.
“A gift economy,” Margot says, “in which the gift is thrown at your head. Mauss would have wept.”
“*Told* you,” says Josie.

A weight comes down over Jack’s head from the side, a long loop of purple beads, and settles on his collar. Laney is facing the avenue again with her arms back in the air. “Don’t make it a thing, fireman,” she tells the float, and goes back to hollering.
He lifts a loop off his collar and looks at it, and leaves it on.

Carrollton ends the way parades end, with a pickup and a man with a push broom, and the crowd doesn’t leave, because King Arthur is due at noon. Its riders are in gold capes and its floats are white and gold under crepe-paper turrets, and the medallion beads come down heavier than Carrollton’s, each with a crown stamped into the metal, so that when one lands on the pavement it rings. Laney catches six cups, two dozen strands and a gold plastic spear with a crown on the grip, and uses the spear to point out ladders. “You. You. *You.*” Cups arrive in their hands.

Across the avenue the piano has found its way back to the top and started over. A crown strand lands on Jude’s hood. He leaves his hands in his pockets and lets it hang there until a toddler on a man’s shoulders points, and then he lowers his head so the man can lift it off. He goes back to standing next to Jack.

By one the avenue has started to drift. A man scrapes his grill. A woman folds a chair and holds it against her chest, looks up the avenue at the next float and then at her husband, and then she’s walking. Half the neutral ground is going home to its televisions with the last float not yet by, a household at a time, shoulders up.
“They’re going to their seats,” Margot says, watching a family collapse a tent. “Whatever chair they had for the Vikings. Josie explained it over eggs. It’s a conservation strategy.”
“Don’t say it out loud,” says Remy, and knocks twice on the hydrant, and the man at the grill knocks on his grill.

“Last one,” Remy announces, to everyone. “Now or never.” The last float is a long time coming. On its top tier a rider in a gold cape is swinging a strand of the heavy beads around his head, searching the crowd for somebody to give it to. On the next ladder Dominic has found his second wind. And at the very back of the float another rider holds up something brown and round in both hands, like a trophy.
“Coconut,” says Remy.
“Zulu’s Mardi Gras morning, Remy,” Josie says.
“Somebody’s holding out.” Under the empty ladder next to them a man in an I WAS THERE FOR THE OVERTIME T-shirt is eating a boudin link, and looking from the coconut to Jack, and back.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself. Sunday on St. Charles he filmed me instead of the floats. Context, he says. He asked how Mass was. He was in the pew.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again. Thursday night at the van she said she wasn’t Western Union and relayed everything anyway. She packed me a bag: FIREMAN, LARGE. Thirty hours. Behave. She told me Julian isn’t coming, like I’d care, and I told her so. Friday night in El Paso she broke a pill in half with her nail. It’s a prescription, Theodore. Saturday on Dupre Street Lena’s mother said So you’re my redhead, and Laney cried in her arms and didn’t say why. Sunday at Carrollton she put a strand of purple beads on me without looking. Don’t make it a thing, fireman. She gave everything else she caught to kids on ladders.

choices.text: Save the best throw you catch for Lena.
choices.key: At Carrollton and King Arthur you caught a medallion bead with a crown on it and saved it for Lena.
response: The rider on the top tier has been looking for somebody the length of the block, and he finds him: a gold glove comes out of the cape, points at the man in the purple beads, and lets go. The strand turns over once in the air, a flash of gold, and Jack’s hand is up and it’s in it. It is heavier than anything else he has caught today, with a crown stamped in the medallion, and he knows where it is going. It goes into the inside pocket of the Carhartt, and he keeps his hand over the outside of the coat through the crush that follows.
Theo sees him do it, and swings the 3GS onto a passing float. Laney, three feet away, says nothing at a volume that carries to the river.

Remy puts a plastic whistle between his teeth and blows until the twins and the redhead and the rich one and the professor and the Ohio boy are all facing him, and then walks backward toward the side street with the milk crate held over his head like a standard, and they follow it.

choices.text: Get into a hollering contest with a nine-year-old.
choices.key: At Carrollton you lost a hollering contest to a nine-year-old. He gave you a cup out of pity.
response: “HEY!” Jack tries, in the voice that has called Rosie in off Glenwood Avenue since she could walk. “UP HERE! HEY!” The flat Youngstown vowels go out over the neutral ground and a pigeon leaves a streetlight.

On the next ladder Dominic fills up until the jersey lifts off his stomach, and lets go. THROW ME SOMETHING, MISTER. The rider on the top tier of the float swings round like he’s been shot at and throws the boy all of it. Margot, who was not asked, rules from the curb that in the literature the elder is expected to lose. Dominic looks down at Jack, kind to the bone, and holds out a pink cup. “You can have this. It’s okay.” He thinks about it. “You’ll get better.”

Remy counts heads at the curb with a finger for each, reaches seven on the second try, and starts them toward the side street with the milk crate on his shoulder, saying the number to himself the length of the block.

choices.text: Climb a stranger’s ladder for the coconut.
choices.key: At Carrollton you climbed a stranger’s ladder for a coconut. It was a stuffed football. Remy called you brother-in-law in front of the whole neutral ground.
response: “Go ahead, young man,” says the man in the overtime shirt, who sets down his boudin and takes hold of the ladder’s legs with both hands. It is made for a seven-year-old’s weight in a seat the size of a mixing bowl. Jack goes up past the third rung to the one under the little seat, one hand on the seat and one in the air, with the neutral ground swaying slightly under him and the rider at the back of the float looking down.

The rider winds up sidearm. The brown thing comes at his chest in a soft arc and he gets both arms round it. It is a stuffed football. There is a fleur-de-lis embroidered on it. It is nothing like a coconut.

The man at the ladder’s foot applauds, hands up high over his head so the neutral ground can see. “Brother-in-law!” Remy yells, at a volume that turns heads on both sides of the avenue, and goes on yelling it. Josie takes one look at him, and takes him by the sleeve and Jude by the hood, and starts for the side street, and the rest of them fall in behind the only one with a plan.
